power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Similarity is fundamental to cognition, shaping both foundational and higher-order processes.

Cognitive theories often adopt a geometric approach, where similarity is defined by the distance or angle between objects in a psychological space, successfully explaining many perceived similarity relations.

However, the validity of such geometric similarity models has been questioned by diverse empirical challenges, such as violations of the metric axioms (minimality, symmetry, and triangle inequality), the common features effect (common features increasing similarity), contextual effects (similarity relations shifting with the presence of other objects), and nearest neighbor effects (single objects considered as most similar to many others).
The present work reviews evidence showing that geometric similarity models can address many of these challenges through psychologically plausible extensions of the model formalizations.
Some extensions add parameters within the standard framework, such as feature-specific attention or object-specific biases (e.g., salience or frequency).

Others generalize the geometric framework itself, through similarity functions that go beyond distances or angles, or psychological spaces that represent objects as something other than points on a multidimensional map.
Each extension addresses specific empirical challenges while maintaining cognitive plausibility.

These findings suggest that geometric models, when appropriately extended, provide a robust foundation for understanding human similarity relations and offer a path toward comprehensive theories of higher-order cognition.
Few concepts in cognitive science have been studied as extensively as similarity.
Similarity in one respect tends to predict similarity in others, and the human mind makes use of this correspondence to interact with the world (Goldstone & Son, 2012).
text.formatted: Similarity in one respect tends to predict similarity in others, and the human mind makes use of this correspondence to interact with the world <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Goldstone & Son, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: For example, people can infer the toxicity of snakes based on their similarity in terms of head shape, pupil shape, and other attributes.

Learning about some venomous snakes allows people to generalize and infer that other, similar snakes are venomous too-even without explicitly knowing rules such as that venomous snakes often have triangular-shaped heads and vertical pupils.

Similarity underlies both perceptual and semantic cognition: it supports processes such as identification (Luce, 1963; Shepard, 1957), categorization (Kruschke, 2008; Nosofsky, 1986), and judgment (Albrecht et al., 2020; Juslin et al., 2003), but also forms the basis of semantic representations (Hintzman, 1984; Landauer & Dumais, 1997) and higher-order reasoning (Hahn & Chater, 1998), problem-solving (Holyoak & Koh, 1987), and memory (Raaijmakers & Shiffrin, 1981).

text.text: Understanding how the human mind perceives similarity is therefore crucial for understanding cognition.
This work examines a seminal framework of psychological similarity-the geometric similarity framework-and addresses the empirical criticisms it has faced.
Specifically, I review evidence showing how psychologically plausible adjustments to formal geometric similarity models can resolve many of these criticisms.

Because similarity is fundamental to cognitive science, various computational models have sought to formalize the underlying cognitive processes (for overviews, see Goldstone & Son, 2012; Hahn, 2014).

text.text: The present work addresses these and related challenges, demonstrating that geometric similarity models can overcome many of the criticisms leveled at them through psychologically plausible extensions.
The following sections formally introduce the two main geometric similarity models, summarize key empirical challenges, and review evidence showing how these challenges can be resolved.
The geometric framework represents each object I as a point in a psychological space, with coordinates corresponding to its attribute values, I = (i 1 , i 2 , . . . , i N ).
Formally, the similarity of object I to object J is a function of their representations, s IJ = f (I, J).

What makes this function geometric is that it depends on I and J only through their spatial relation in psychological space: either the distance between them (distance-based similarity, s dist IJ ) or the angle between them (angle-based similarity, s cos IJ ).
Throughout this article, s IJ without superscript refers to either form.

Distance-based similarity dominates in classic perceptual models of stimulus identification, recognition, and categorization (e.g., Nosofsky, 1986; Shepard, 1987), where similarity depends on attribute differences and overall magnitude-objects are more similar the closer they are in psychological space.

text.text: In contrast, angle-based similarity is more common in semantic models of language and memory (e.g., Hintzman, 1984; Landauer & Dumais, 1997), which often assume high-dimensional psychological spaces where similarity depends on attribute patterns rather than magnitude.

text.text: The most widely used measure defines similarity as the cosine of this angle.

Formally, the cosine similarity s cos IJ between objects I and J is given by where I • J denotes the dot product of vectors I and J, ∥I∥ and ∥J∥ represent their respective Euclidean norms, and θ is the angle between I and J. Intuitively, cosine similarity measures the directional alignment of two vectors-their dot product captures how closely they point in the same direction, while normalization by their magnitudes ensures that only the angle between the vectors, not their lengths, influences similarity.
Cosine similarity can be computed directly from attribute values without explicitly calculating the angle θ first.
Nevertheless, θ can be recovered via θ = arccos s cos IJ .
Like distance d IJ , θ can be treated as a metric, satisfying analogous assumptions (see below).

By relying on the location of objects in a psychological space, geometric similarity models make a series of assumptions that have faced empirical criticism (Goldstone & Son, 2012).

text.text: One key assumption is that the cognitive system represents objects as vectors of distinct attributes, each assigned a numeric value. Tversky (1977) argued that this so-called dimensional assumption may apply to some objects, like colors or geometric figures, but not to others, like countries or personalities, which might be better represented by qualitative features rather than quantitative dimensions (see the discussion for more details).

text.text: The primary focus of this article, however, lies in the assumptions about how similarity is computed provided that objects can be represented as vectors of attribute values.

In particular, geometric models assume metric axioms (minimality, symmetry, and triangle inequality) which restrict the possible similarity spaces (Beals et al., 1968; Krantz et al., 1971; Tversky & Krantz, 1970).

text.text: These assumptions have been questioned on empirical grounds using various methods that measure psychological similarity directly or infer it from similarity-based cognition tasks (Daggett & Hout, 2025; Tversky, 1977).

text.text: Direct measures include pairwise similarity ratings, in which participants judge the similarity of two objects on a scale; free associations, in which participants list the words most similar to a reference word; and choice tasks, in which participants select the most similar stimuli from a small set (including triad tasks, in which participants select the two most similar of three stimuli, or, if one stimulus serves as a reference, which of the remaining two is more similar to it).

Indirect tasks, by contrast, infer similarity from related but distinct choice behavior: in object identification tasks, similarity is inferred from confusion patterns as participants name individual objects, and in same-different tasks, similarity is inferred from accuracy and response times as participants decide whether two stimuli are the same.

The underlying idea is that objects often confused with each other or requiring long response times to discriminate are likely to be psychologically similar, whereas dissimilar objects can be told apart quickly and accurately.

However, performance in such similarity-based cognition tasks may reflect both properties of similarity itself and additional task-specific processes (e.g., response biases), either of which can produce violations of the assumptions of geometric models-a distinction that recurs throughout this review.

Taken together, these findings suggest that self-similarity can differ between objects and that an object can even appear more similar to another object than to itself-provided that these patterns reflect similarity rather than task-specific processes.
Another assumption of geometric similarity models is symmetry (Beals et al., 1968): the distance (or angle) between objects is non-directional, formally d IJ = d JI , directly implying s IJ = s JI .

text.text: Symmetry reflects insensitivity to the direction of comparison-the same psychological similarity is formed irrespective of which of two objects serves as subject or referent.
Geometric similarity models thus do not differentiate between "the similarity of I to J", "the similarity of J to I", and "the similarity between I and J" (Tversky, 1977).

text.text: His featural framework posits that two objects' common features increase their similarity, whereas each object's distinctive features (i.e., features present in one object but not the other) decrease similarity. Tversky (1977) formalized two main models in this framework: the contrast model, which computes a weighted difference between common and distinctive features, and the ratio model, which computes the proportion of common features relative to the total number of common and distinctive features.

text.text: These formulations naturally account for several key violations of geometric axioms.
For example, asymmetry arises because the distinctive features of each object can be weighted differently, making similarity directional.

Specifically, by assuming that the mind weights distinctive features of the subject of comparison (i.e., I in "the similarity of I to J") more strongly than those of the object of comparison (i.e., J in the example above), the featural framework can explain why less salient items with fewer distinctive features are judged more similar to salient, distinctive items than vice versa.

The trade-off between common and distinctive features can also account for violations of the nearest neighbor bound: A prototypical or superordinate object tends to have few distinctive features of its own while sharing many common features with its instances, allowing it to attain high similarity to a large number of instances simultaneously-unconstrained by the dimensionality limits that bound geometric models (Tversky & Hutchinson, 1986).

text.text: Furthermore, the common features effect is explained straightforwardly by the featural framework, in which similarity increases with the number of common features.
Tversky showed that this relationship can be predicted from the features people list, in particular when weighting features by their frequency of mention.

People also tend to weight common features more when judging similarity and distinctive features more when judging difference, questioning the extent to which similarity and difference judgments are exact opposites.
Moreover, Tversky (1977) also showed that feature weighting is context-dependent, shifting with the set of presented objects, making features become more or less diagnostic for a task.

text.text: The work of Tversky demonstrated that many empirical phenomena can be captured by adopting a different, feature-based representation, in which feature matching (i.e., identifying two objects' common and distinctive features) determines similarity.
An alternative approach, however, is to retain geometric representations while extending them to accommodate the empirical limitations reviewed above.
In the following sections, I review how geometric similarity models can address these limitations through psychologically plausible modifications to their formalization.
These extensions help bridge the gap between theoretical assumptions and empirical findings, offering a refined framework for understanding psychological similarity.
To overcome the empirical challenges of geometric similarity models, psychological research has proposed a number of extensions to its formalizations.

These extensions aim not only to account for violations of the assumptions described above but also to be psychologically plausible and cognitively interpretable while remaining in a geometric framework.

This review discusses four model extensions: attribute-specific weights, reflecting how attention is distributed across attributes when objects are compared; object-specific biases, capturing that some objects exert greater influence on similarity-based cognition, for instance due to their salience, frequency, or typicality; generalized similarity functions, which incorporate geometric aspects beyond distances or angles in similarity computation; and generalized psychological spaces, which represent objects in ways beyond points in a multidimensional map.

Some empirical challenges of geometric similarity models can be addressed by introducing a vector of attribute-specific parameters w = (w 1 , . . . , w N ) that weight the contribution of individual attributes to similarity.

In distance-based similarities, the weights are multiplied with the attribute differences between objects (Eq. 1), yielding the weighted Minkowski distance (Carroll & Chang, 1970) where w n denotes the weight assigned to the difference | i n -j n | of attribute n (with0 ≤ w n ≤ 1 and n w n = 1).

text.text: Two implications follow.

First, the account turns the sum-to-one constraint, introduced above for identifiability, into a substantive psychological assumption: Attention is a limited resource, so attending to a new attribute comes at the expense of the others.

Second, unlike the contrast model, in which a common feature adds a constant amount of similarity, the account predicts that the common features effect depends on how much the objects otherwise differ-a so far untested way to distinguish the two accounts.
Thus, while common features can enhance similarity directly, as Tversky argued, they can also do so indirectly by diverting attention away from differing attributes.

Attention mechanisms can also account for the extralist feature effect (Osth et al., 2023), a context effect in recognition memory previously considered incompatible with geometric similarity models (Johns & Mewhort, 2002; Mewhort & Johns, 2000 , 2005).

Notably, the extralist feature effect emerged for separable attributes but not for integral attributes, likely because allocating attention to individual attributes is more challenging in the latter case.
Implications for metric structure.

So far, attention weights have been assumed to change at most between contexts-for instance, across trials, as in the extralist feature effect-but to remain constant within a context, such that all comparisons within a trial use the same weights regardless of which objects are compared.
This raises a more general question: At what grain does attention vary?
It may be a stable property of a person (Carroll & Chang, 1970), shift across trials or contexts (Osth et al., 2023), or even change from one comparison to the next within a trial.

text.text: As long as attention is constant within a context, the weighted Minkowski distance satisfies all metric axioms: it is minimal for identical objects, symmetric, and satisfies triangle inequality.

However, relaxing this assumption by allowing attention to vary across comparisons within a context has important implications for the model's metric structure, permitting violations of symmetry and triangle inequality (but not minimality; Micko & Fischer, 1970; Shepard, 1964).

text.text: Summary.

In summary, attribute-specific attention parameters have a long-standing tradition in geometric similarity models and provide a unifying account for the common features effect (Seitz, 2023), contextual effects (e.g., Osth et al., 2023), and certain violations of metric axioms (Micko & Fischer, 1970).

text.text: Another extension that can address violations of the assumptions underlying geometric similarity models is the inclusion of bias parameters b = (b J , b K , . . . ), associated with objects J, K, . . . .

Unlike attribute weights, which enter the similarity computation itself, these biases have classically been part of models of similarity-based cognition, such as identification and categorization, where they help map similarities onto responses.

text.text: Relation to a general class of proximity models.
So far, biases have entered at the level of similarity-based cognition.
To better understand their role for similarity, it is useful to consider a more general class of proximity models.

text.text: Because it models similarity judgments rather than only identification data, it addresses whether bias-like extensions are needed to capture similarity per se, not merely response processes in identification tasks.

In the distance-density model, the psychological distance between I and J is given by where d IJ is the Minkowski distance as computed in Eq. 1, δ I ≥ 0 is the spatial density around object I in psychological space, typically defined as the number of neighboring objects within a fixed radius, and α and β are weighting factors for the density terms.

Objects surrounded by many neighbors are perceived as less similar to each other than their raw geometric distance suggests-intuitively, a crowded region of psychological space makes objects feel separated by many other objects.

text.text: In sum, biases can capture psychological properties of individual objects (e.g., their frequency, typicality, salience, or density).

Incorporating bias terms allows geometric similarity models to account for violations of minimality, symmetry, and nearest neighbor relations (Krumhansl, 1978; Nosofsky, 1991) and reveals strong conceptual links to featural approaches to similarity (cf. Tversky, 1977).

text.text: The extensions discussed so far keep the geometric similarity function and add parameters to it: Attention weights rescale the psychological space, and biases enter at the level of similarity-based cognition.
A third extension modifies the similarity function itself, generalizing it to functions with weaker mathematical assumptions.

Tversky's contrast model could also be counted among them, but as shown above, it can equally be expressed as a symmetric similarity plus object biases, and it departs from geometric models mainly in its representation (feature sets rather than points; see General Discussion).
This section therefore focuses on functions directly derived from Euclidean distances, which remain among the most widely used similarity models in both psychology and machine learning.

One simple approach is to use the dot product between vectors, which links Euclidean distances and cosine similarity but allows for varying self-similarities: Because the dot product of a vector with itself equals its squared length, objects with different vector lengths can differ in self-similarity, predicting violations of minimality.
For example, objects with large attribute values are predicted to exhibit higher self-similarity than more moderate objects, akin to increased salience.

Beyond dot products, Euclidean distances can be generalized to other functional forms that do not necessarily satisfy all geometric assumptions.
I will now review two prominent generalizations: the squared Euclidean distance and the Mahalanobis distance.
Squared Euclidean distance.
The squared Euclidean distance arises in the geometric similarity model by setting r = 2 in Eq. 1 and squaring the result.

text.text: Unlike the squared Euclidean distance, the Mahalanobis distance incorporates variability information about the distribution from which the compared objects originate.
Intuitively, it measures the number of standardized units by which one object differs from another within a given category distribution.

Formally, the (squared) Mahalanobis distance d 2 IJ∈J of object I to object J from category J is given by where Σ -1 J is the inverse of the variance-covariance matrix for category J to which object J belongs.
Σ J contains in its main diagonal the attribute variances and in its off-diagonal cells the pairwise attribute covariances (i.e., the unstandardized correlations) in category J .
By using the inverse of the matrix, the Mahalanobis distance divides the attribute differences by the attribute variances and covariances.
Variances and covariances affect the Mahalanobis distance in distinct ways (see Figure 7).

text.text: Larger attribute variances lead to smaller distances, as the objects are considered fewer standardized units apart.
Stronger correlations reduce the Mahalanobis distance when the differences between the objects align with the correlations but increase it when differences and correlations do not align.
If Σ J is an identity matrix (i.e., variances of 1 and correlations of 0), Eq. 13 simplifies to the squared Euclidean distance.

text.text: Psychologically, this reflects that I appears relatively similar to J, as J stems from category J known to vary a lot, whereas J appears relatively dissimilar to I, as I stems from category I known to vary little.
Correlations can also lead to asymmetries.
If two categories differ in the strength of their attribute correlations, then the similarity between two objects, one from each category, is generally asymmetric.

Even if two categories have attribute correlations of identical strength, asymmetric similarities result if the correlations differ in direction (i.e., a positive correlation in one category and a negative correlation in the other).
If the same variance-covariance matrix applies to both objects, their similarity is always symmetric.
Admittedly, this account of asymmetry requires that the compared objects are evaluated against different reference distributions.
This may be common, however, as objects are typically encountered as instances of broader categories whose variability can enter the comparison.
A weight difference of 10 kg, for instance, seems unremarkable between two dogs but enormous between two cats, because dogs vary far more in size.
Accordingly, the account predicts that a wolf appears more similar to a dog-a referent from a highly variable category-than a dog appears to a wolf.

Whether people indeed scale differences by the variability associated with the referent when judging similarity remains to be tested; so far, evidence for this mechanism comes mainly from categorization.

text.text: A final extension involves generalized geometric spaces, which move beyond the usual Euclidean representation.
Instead of representing objects as points in a standard metric space, generalized spaces allow for more flexible representations.
This flexibility can be especially useful for modeling psychological phenomena such as asymmetries, contextual effects, and nearest neighbor effects.

One approach discussed in the literature is the use of Hilbert spaces (Jäkel et al., 2008), a geometric space that provides the basis for a quantum geometric model of similarity (Pothos et al., 2013).

In recent years, Hilbert spaces have been used to develop the quantum model of geometric similarity (Pothos et al., 2013).
text.formatted: In recent years, Hilbert spaces have been used to develop the quantum model of geometric similarity <ref type="bibr" target="#b138">(Pothos et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: A key difference to the traditional geometric model is that objects are not interpreted as individual points in space but as subspaces of varying dimensionality.
Each dimension of such a subspace denotes a set of features associated with the respective object.
Accordingly, the more one knows about an object, the greater the dimensionality of the subspace representing the object in Hilbert space.
If different objects share some features, their subspaces in Hilbert space will overlap.

At any moment in time, a person's thoughts can be represented by a unit-length state vector; the degree of correspondence between the state vector and a specific object I can then be measured by projecting the state vector onto the object's subspace.
Geometrically, projection means that the perpendicular is dropped from the state vector onto the subspace.

This corresponds to computing the part of the state vector contained in the subspace, which is mathematically achieved by multiplying the outer product II ⊤ of the subspace dimensions I with the state vector X (that is, II ⊤ X) 9 .
text.formatted: This corresponds to computing the part of the state vector contained in the subspace, which is mathematically achieved by multiplying the outer product II ⊤ of the subspace dimensions I with the state vector X (that is, II ⊤ X) <ref type="foot" target="#foot_6">9</ref> .

text.text: The quantum similarity between two objects I and J is then based on the subsequent projection of the state vector X to the subspace of the first object I and from there to the subspace of the second object J. Specifically, the quantum similarity between I and J equals the squared length of the subsequent projections, JJ ⊤ II ⊤ X 2.

Note that this measure of similarity is a squared length: In the simplest case of one-dimensional subspaces, it equals the product of the squared cosines between the state vector and I and between I and J, and thus generalizes cosine similarity.
It can be interpreted as the probability of thinking about one object from the perspective of another object (Pothos et al., 2013; Trueblood et al., 2014).

text.text: In addition to triangle and corner inequality violations, the model can predict asymmetric similarities.
Specifically, it can predict Tversky's (1977) finding that objects about which people have little knowledge are more similar to objects about which people know a lot than vice versa.

text.text: The quantum model represents the amount of knowledge about an object by the dimensionality of its subspace and predicts that objects with lower-dimensional subspaces are more similar to objects with higher-dimensional subspaces than vice versa, because projecting from a lower-to a higher-dimensional subspace retains more of the state vector's amplitude than vice versa (see Pothos et al., 2013, Fig. 2).

text.text: One important prerequisite for this is that the two subspaces are neither identical nor orthogonal: Identical subspaces denote identical objects, for which asymmetric similarities make conceptually no sense; orthogonal subspaces, in turn, denote objects with opposite features and with a similarity of 0 in either comparison direction.
Using the quantum approach, Pothos et al. (2013) discuss the famous example of Tversky (1977), according to which Korea is more similar to China than the other way round.

text.text: Because people in general have a greater range of knowledge about China than about Korea, China will be represented by a subspace of larger dimensionality than Korea.
Furthermore, the two subspaces will be related to each other and overlap without being completely identical (in other words, China and Korea have similar, but not identical features).
The greater similarity from Korea to China than vice versa will now naturally emerge in the quantum model by the sequential projection of the state vector.
Finally, the quantum model can also predict contextual effects on similarity (Yearsley et al., 2022), including the diagnosticity effect (Pothos et al., 2013).

The quantum model explains the diagnosticity effect by incorporating the influence of the contextual objects into the computation of similarity.
Reconsider people's tendency to select Sweden as most similar to Austria when the other options are Hungary and Poland.

To compute an option's similarity to Austria, the model projects the state vector onto the two other options (in both possible orders), then onto the option itself, and finally onto Austria, averaging over both orders.
Each projection between dissimilar countries (small subspace overlap) loses much of the state vector's length, whereas projections between similar countries retain most of it.

For Sweden, both sequences (Hungary → Poland → Sweden → Austria and Poland → Hungary → Sweden → Austria) contain the length-preserving projection between the similar countries Hungary and Poland and only one length-reducing projection to Sweden.

For Hungary, in contrast, one sequence (Poland → Sweden → Hungary → Austria) detours via Sweden and thus contains two length-reducing projections, lowering Hungary's average similarity to Austria (and likewise for Poland).

Through this mechanism, the quantum model predicts diagnosticity effects-the key factor is a direct projection between highly-overlapping subspaces of two choice options that makes the remaining, distinct choice option appear more similar to the reference stimulus.
Other non-Euclidean geometry.
In addition to Hilbert spaces, other non-Euclidean geometry can be used to create generalized psychological spaces.
While Euclidean spaces are flat and lack curvature (resulting in planes such as a map when considering two dimensions), these non-Euclidean spaces have curvature.
Positive curvature leads to elliptic surfaces (e.g., the sphere of the Earth); negative curvature results in hyperbolic surfaces (e.g., a saddle shape).

Although such non-Euclidean spaces are frequently used in computer science to model non-Euclidean distances and similarity relations (Nickel & Kiela, 2017; Peng et al., 2021; Wilson et al., 2010), their application in psychology has only recently gained attention.
text.formatted: Although such non-Euclidean spaces are frequently used in computer science to model non-Euclidean distances and similarity relations <ref type="bibr" target="#b114">(Nickel & Kiela, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b134">Peng et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b200">Wilson et al., 2010)</ref>, their application in psychology has only recently gained attention.

text.text: Roads and Love (2024) discuss the Poincaré space, a hyperbolic space which expands exponentially as one moves away from its center.
For two dimensions, this hyperbolic space can be mapped onto the interior of a circle (the Poincaré disk), with the edges representing points infinitely far away.
As one moves from the center of the disk toward its edges, the distance increases exponentially.
Thus, objects close to the center have a small distance, while objects near the edges have a large distance.

Because of this exponential growth, Poincaré space is particularly effective at representing hierarchical similarity relations (Klimovskaia et al., 2020; Nickel & Kiela, 2017): The generic term (e.g., fruit) is located at the origin, with the specific instances (e.g., apple) surrounding it.
text.formatted: Because of this exponential growth, Poincaré space is particularly effective at representing hierarchical similarity relations <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">(Klimovskaia et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b114">Nickel & Kiela, 2017)</ref>: The generic term (e.g., fruit) is located at the origin, with the specific instances (e.g., apple) surrounding it.

text.text: In Poincaré space, the number of nearest neighbors that can fit around the origin increases exponentially as one moves further from the origin, enabling a more flexible representation of hierarchical structures compared to Euclidean space.

In this way, Poincaré and other hyperbolic spaces can accommodate tree-like structures (as in e.g., Carroll, 1976; Cunningham, 1978; Sattath & Tversky, 1977), accounting for why some objects are the nearest neighbor of more other objects than is possible in Euclidean geometry.

text.text: In sum, generalized geometric spaces extend beyond traditional map-like mental representations.

For example, Hilbert spaces, which form the basis of quantum approaches to geometric similarity, can predict violations of triangle inequality and symmetry as well as contextual effects (Pothos et al., 2013).

Specifically, I considered additional free parameters in the form of attribute attention and object biases as well as generalized similarity functions and psychological spaces.

text.text: Yet, addressing more violations does not make an extension better, as some violations may be more frequent or more important than others.
Moreover, the mere fact that an extension can predict a particular violation does not guarantee that it captures the violation in the correct way.

The aim of this paper is therefore to propose plausible model extensions that appear to be suitable candidates for explaining human similarity data-whether they succeed must be evaluated on a case-by-case basis.

Violations are task-and material-dependent, not universal.
The overview of empirical challenges showed that while people sometimes violate the assumptions of the geometric framework, these violations are not universal.

For example, although minimality is occasionally violated in identification tasks (e.g., when people confuse one object with another), it is generally satisfied in similarity judgment tasks, which arguably capture similarity relations most directly.

Similarly, Tversky and Hutchinson (1986) found that while nearest neighbor analyses occasionally exceeded geometric limits in conceptual data sets with generic terms, they generally fell within the admissible range for perceptual data lacking generic terms.

text.text: Thus, violations of the assumptions of geometric similarities are task-and material-dependent rather than universal.
Even when people violate the geometric assumptions, these violations can often be addressed within the geometric framework through psychologically plausible extensions.
Many extensions incorporate established psychological constructs, such as attention and biases toward certain response options, which are central to similarity-based cognition.
Notably, some extensions were not originally proposed to address geometric violations but to model broader cognitive processes.

For example, attribute-specific attention, prominently used to capture selective attention to diagnostic attributes in categorization tasks (see Fig. 5b), also addresses various violations of the assumptions of geometric similarity models.

Object-specific biases are most critical for identification and confusion data, where responses reflect not only similarity but also the salience of the response options (Corter, 1987; Nosofsky, 1991), and attribute-specific weights are particularly important for categorization tasks with differentially diagnostic attributes (Nosofsky, 1986).

text.text: The extensions thus become necessary when the paradigm introduces additional factors that a purely geometric account cannot absorb.
The reviewed extensions also differ in how much flexibility they add to the model.
Attribute-specific attention and object-specific biases typically introduce free parameters that are estimated from the data.

Generalized similarity functions and psychological spaces may also come with parameters, but some of these can be derived a priori rather than fitted, such as the attribute variances and correlations entering the Mahalanobis distance, which can be computed from the stimulus distributions.

In either case, model comparison methods that account for model flexibility, such as cross-validation, allow testing whether an extension captures something psychologically meaningful or merely increases overfitting.
In sum, this review demonstrates that no single extension accounts for all violations.
Instead, a combination of the extensions-to be chosen based on the observed violations-can effectively address these challenges.
While this review has focused on the empirical challenges of geometric approaches to similarity, it has largely assumed that objects can be represented as points in a multidimensional space.

However, this dimensional assumption itself can be questioned: Tversky (1977) argued that it suits simple perceptual stimuli such as colors, which vary continuously along a few dimensions; complex stimuli such as faces or personalities, by contrast, seem to consist of many qualitative features and cannot easily be represented as points in a psychological space.

text.text: More generally, a growing body of work demonstrates that natural language processing and vision models can construct high-dimensional geometric representations of complex stimuli, which can then serve as psychological spaces for modeling similarity as well as judgment and decision-making more generally.

Specifically, pre-trained neural networks produce embedding spaces in which geometric proximity corresponds to meaningful similarity, making standard functions such as cosine similarity and Euclidean distance directly applicable (Reimers & Gurevych, 2019; Roads & Love, 2024).

Scenarios with similar vector representations were also rated similarly by participants-although these judgments were not used to derive the embedding.

On a larger scale, the computational processes underlying similarity are directly linked to the psychological space on which similarity operates-any similarity function presupposes some representational format, and conversely, any set of representations implies a corresponding comparison process (Roads & Love, 2024).

text.text: So far, the present work has taken the geometric representation as given and sought to extend or modify the similarity function operating on it: adding bias or density terms to account for asymmetry (Krumhansl, 1978; Nosofsky, 1991), introducing dynamic attribute weighting to account for context effects (Goldstone et al., 1997; Kruschke, 1992), or replacing Euclidean distances and spaces with generalized geometry to accommodate violations of the metric axioms (Pothos et al., 2013; Sakamoto et al., 2008).

text.text: An alternative strategy, however, is to adopt non-geometric psychological spaces whose associated comparison processes can predict these empirical limitations naturally, without requiring post-hoc modifications to the similarity function.

I therefore now consider featural models (Tversky, 1977), probabilistic and topic-based models (Griffiths et al., 2007), neural network-based distributed representations (Roads & Love, 2024), and transformational and alignment-based models (Hahn et al., 2003; Markman & Gentner, 1993).

text.text: The simplest departure from geometric space is the set-theoretic representation, in which objects are encoded as collections of discrete features rather than as points in a continuous space (Tversky, 1977).

(2007) proposed a probabilistic account of semantic association, in which each word is represented as a probability distribution over latent topics that capture patterns of co-occurrence across language, and the association between two words is given by the conditional probability of one word given the other.

(2007)</ref> proposed a probabilistic account of semantic association, in which each word is represented as a probability distribution over latent topics that capture patterns of co-occurrence across language, and the association between two words is given by the conditional probability of one word given the other.

text.text: Because conditional probabilities are directional and need not satisfy metric constraints, the topic model naturally accommodates the key violations observed in free-association data: asymmetries (e.g., "text" elicits "book" more often than the reverse, because "text" shares its topics with "book", while "book" also occurs in topics beyond those of "text"), triangle inequality violations (e.g., "bank" shares financial topics with "money" and geographical topics with "river", while "money" and "river" share few topics), and violations of the nearest neighbor bound (e.g., a general word like "animal" occurs broadly across many topics and is thus probable given many specific instances).

In this respect, topic models resemble a probabilistic variant of Tversky's (1977) featural framework, in which topics play the role of features and similarity reflects the degree to which two words overlap in topics.

text.text: A more substantive departure from geometric space is the graph-based representation, in which objects are encoded as nodes and their relations as directed or weighted edges.

Here the representational format is inherently non-metric: there is no assumption of continuity or dimensionality in the underlying space, and similarity is measured through processes such as spreading activation, shortest-path, or graph edit distance.

In semantic networks derived from free associations, for instance, the proximity of two concepts can be defined via the shortest path between them (Kumar et al., 2020) or via random walks that integrate over all paths between them, discounting longer ones (De Deyne et al., 2016).

text.text: A further development of this idea is constituted by (neural) networks, which can be viewed as weighted graphs.

In the previous section, pre-trained networks served only as a tool to obtain geometric psychological spaces; here, the network itself is treated as a model of how similarity is represented and computed.

Unlike graph models, which explicitly encode relations, networks learn distributed representations implicitly from data, encoding objects as high-dimensional activation patterns whose structure emerges from training (Hinton, 1989).

text.text: Similarity is then measured in the resulting embedding space-via cosine similarity, dot products, or learned metric functions.

The contrast to the geometric approach is thus not one of geometric versus non-geometric representations: whereas geometric models combine a fixed space with a separately specified similarity function, networks learn the representation and the similarity function jointly (Roads & Love, 2024).

text.text: Neural network approaches, while powerful, face a challenge of opacity: the learned representations are difficult to interpret, making it hard to determine whether a good fit reflects genuine psychological insight or simply the flexibility of a high-dimensional model (Roads & Love, 2024).

text.text: Graph-based and distributed representations can naturally accommodate for some empirical challenges such as asymmetric similarity judgments.

Spreading activation models (Anderson, 1983; Collins & Loftus, 1975) produce asymmetries because activation spreads from a cue node along weighted edges, so the similarity from I to J depends on the outgoing path structure from I, which differs from that of J-a mechanism that explains classic priming asymmetries like "canary" priming "bird" faster than vice versa.

text.text: While geometric models treat features as unstructured and independent of one another, many features have spatial or temporal relationships (e.g., one feature is to the left of another) or hierarchical relationships (e.g., one feature is part of another).
To account for such structure, alignment and transformational models of similarity have been developed.
Alignment models align the parts of objects based on their roles within each object.

For example, when comparing two stimuli consisting of three circles of varying sizes each, the smallest circle in one object is aligned with the smallest circle in the other, even if in absolute size it more closely matches another circle (Markman & Gentner, 1993).

text.text: Taken together, this comparison across frameworks suggests that no single approach account for perceived similarity optimally across all stimulus domains and task paradigms.
Featural models excel for discrete feature sets but may be less suited to continuous perceptual domains.
Probabilistic topic models handle semantic violations elegantly but are largely restricted to language.
Network models are flexible but often opaque.

The geometric framework offers a unified and interpretable account across perceptual and conceptual domains, but its adequacy depends on appropriate extensions to address the violations observed in a given task and stimulus set.
Geometric similarity models are probably the most influential yet also the most controversially discussed framework of psychological similarity.

They are widely used in theories of higher-order cognition (e.g., identification and categorization, language, and memory) and in multivariate statistics and machine learning (e.g., multidimensional scaling and clustering), but they also face a range of empirical challenges, as humans can violate the assumptions they rely on.
This review demonstrated that many of these challenges can be addressed within the geometric framework through psychologically compelling model extensions.

Although not the only viable account of psychological similarity, the geometric framework, when appropriately extended, remains a principled, interpretable, and competitive account-and its empirical limitations are now well-characterized enough to guide the selection of extensions on a case-by-case basis.

The diversity of psychological similarity reflects the complexity of human cognition, underscoring the need for flexible formal frameworks that adapt to the nuanced ways cognitive systems perceive similarity.

This review has two interrelated aims.
The first is descriptive: to systematically map which empirical violations of geometric assumptions can be addressed by which model extensions, and under what conditions.

The second is normative: to argue that the geometric framework, when appropriately extended, remains a viable and competitive account of psychological similarity-not merely as a default assumption inherited from psychophysics, but as a theoretically principled choice with distinct advantages.

Geometric models constitute arguably the most prominent framework to investigate similarity: For instance, multidimensional scaling infers an embedding in which geometric distances correspond as closely as possible to human similarity ratings (Shepard, 1962a (Shepard, , 1962b)), and it provided the basis for many similarity-based models of higher-order cognition (e.g., Nosofsky, 1986)-illustrating the deep connection between geometric similarities, cognitive models, and machine learning algorithms.

text.text: I see three principal reasons to adopt a geometric representation as the starting point, which I discuss in turn below.

First, violations of the geometric assumptions are task-and material-dependent rather than universal, and geometric representations are particularly well-suited to paradigms in which stimuli vary continuously along identifiable dimensions-colors, tones, sizes, orientations.

Second, the geometric framework offers strong psychological interpretability: similarities such as dot products are easy to compute, distances and angles are intuitive, and the extensions reviewed here map cleanly onto established psychological constructs.

Third, and most practically, modern behavioral and computational methods can derive geometric representations for complex, naturalistic stimuli such as everyday objects, faces, and semantic concepts (Battleday et al., 2020; Hebart et al., 2020; Nosofsky et al., 2017; Nosofsky et al., 2018; Roads & Love, 2021 , 2024; Smits et al., 2002).
